title: A troubleshooting decision tree for a VFD that trips on overvoltage during decel
summary: Fast branch structure for a VFD overvoltage trip on deceleration — short headings, not an essay.

blocks.title: OV on decel — branch, do not essay
blocks.body: The drive trips on overvoltage while slowing down. That usually means the DC bus is climbing faster than the brake path can absorb regenerated energy. Work the tree top-down.

items.label: Typical fault code family — confirm on your drive
Trip timing: during slowdown, not at steady speed
Motor acting as generator into the DC bus

blocks.heading: 30-second cabinet scan
blocks.body: Before changing parameters: read the keypad fault text, glance at the brake resistor (if present) for heat discoloration, and note whether the trip happened on a commanded stop or a speed change mid-cycle. Those three observations pick the starting branch faster than a manual chapter.

nodes.title: A. Confirm timing
nodes.detail: Trip only on decel / stop? If it also trips at constant speed, leave this page — look at line spikes and braking resistor wiring differently.

nodes.title: B. Load inertia & decel time
nodes.detail: High inertia + aggressive decel ⇒ lots of regen. Lengthen decel or use coast-to-stop if process allows.

nodes.title: C. Brake hardware present?
nodes.detail: No resistor / brake chopper ⇒ bus has nowhere to go. Add rated dynamic braking or slow the stop.

nodes.title: D. Resistor & wiring OK?
nodes.detail: Open resistor, wrong ohms, loose lug, or chopper fault ⇒ OV returns. Measure cold resistance; inspect thermal switch.

nodes.title: E. Parameters
nodes.detail: Brake enable, duty cycle limits, overvoltage stall prevention / regen avoidance features — match the manual for your model.

nodes.title: F. Mechanical drag
nodes.detail: Failing bearings or seized load can change the energy story — but if the trip is cleanly on commanded decel, stay on A–E first.

blocks.heading: Why decel makes voltage climb
blocks.body: When you command a fast stop, the motor's rotating mass keeps delivering energy into the drive. The inverter's diodes dump that energy onto the DC bus capacitors. Without a path through a brake chopper into a resistor (or a regen unit back to the line), bus voltage rises until the protection trips. Stretching decel reduces the power (energy per time). Braking hardware raises how much power you can absorb.

blocks.title: Not this tree
blocks.body: Undervoltage, ground faults, overcurrent on accel, and encoder loss are different animals. If the code is not an overvoltage family fault tied to slowing down, put this page down.

blocks.heading: Branch A — Prove it is a decel OV
items: Note the exact fault code and whether it appears on STOP, on a speed decrease, or also at steady RPM.
If possible, trend DC bus voltage while decelerating — a climb into the OV threshold seals the diagnosis.
If trips happen at constant speed or on power-up, stop this tree and pursue line quality / miswiring.

blocks.heading: Branch B — Soften the stop
items: Double the decel time as a test. If OV disappears, you confirmed excess regen rate.
Ask process whether a longer stop is acceptable. If not, you need braking hardware, not wishful parameters.
Try coast-to-stop (if safe for the machine) to prove the drive is healthy when it is not absorbing regen.

columns.name: No brake resistor
columns.detail: Options: lengthen decel, reduce inertia (process), add chopper+resistor sized for stop energy, or a regen unit on large systems.

columns.name: Resistor installed
columns.detail: Verify enable bits, ohm value vs. drive minimum, continuous/peak watt rating, and that the thermal switch is in the right input.

columns.name: Shared / external brake
columns.detail: Confirm this drive is actually connected to the shared resistor network and not orphaned by a contactor.

items.label: Measure resistor cold ohms
items.detail: Compare to nameplate. Open = definite OV on any serious decel.

items.label: Inspect lugs and chopper terminals
items.detail: Heat-discolored hardware is a clue; so is a wire on the wrong terminal.

items.label: Check brake transistor / chopper fault history
items.detail: Some drives log brake IGBT faults separately from OV.

items.label: Confirm duty cycle vs. how often you stop
items.detail: A resistor rated for occasional stops will cook on cyclic high-inertia indexing.

blocks.heading: Branch E — Parameter suspects (names vary)
rows: Odd regen behavior; fix data anyway
blocks.caption: Use your drive manual's exact parameter numbers. This table is a hunt list, not a programming sheet.

items.title: Energy math
items.detail: If still failing, size braking for stop energy or change the mechanical stop method.

blocks.title: Lockout before you touch brake wiring
blocks.body: DC bus capacitors hold charge after power-down. Follow the drive's discharge wait time. Overvoltage troubleshooting does not require live terminal exploration.

blocks.heading: Branch check
blocks.prompt: OV occurs only when stopping a high-inertia fan. Lengthening decel from 5 s to 20 s clears the fault. No brake resistor is installed. Best next step for production-speed stops?
options: Ignore it — 20 s stops are fine forever without asking operations
Add properly sized dynamic braking (or approved regen) if process needs a faster stop
Raise the OV trip threshold in a hidden menu
blocks.explanation: The test proved regen rate was the issue. If the process needs a fast stop, absorb the energy with rated hardware rather than hiding the trip.
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes — match braking hardware to the stop the process actually needs.
blocks.wrongFeedback: Branch B explained the test; Branch C covers what to add when time alone is not acceptable.

blocks.heading: Leave with a written branch
blocks.body: Record which node cleared the fault. The next tech should not have to rediscover whether it was decel time or an open resistor.
